note.explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because it is moving. Potential energy is stored energy due to a body's position or deformation. Near the Earth, a raised body's gravitational potential energy is found using Eₚ = mgh.
examples: A moving truck has kinetic energy.
A block held above the ground has gravitational potential energy.
note.checkAnswer: The body's gravitational potential energy is 60 J.
note.simple: Energy is the ability to do work. Motion gives a body kinetic energy; height or deformation can give it potential energy.

written.text: Can the kinetic energy of a body ever be negative?
written.finalAnswer: No; kinetic energy cannot be negative because Eₖ = ½mv², and mass and the square of velocity are non-negative.

rubric.why: The answer must correctly state whether negative kinetic energy is possible.
The relation explains why kinetic energy cannot be negative.
rubric.how: Use Eₖ = ½mv² and note that v² cannot be negative.

modelAnswer: Eₖ = ½mv², and mass and the square of velocity are non-negative; therefore, kinetic energy cannot be negative.

written.text: Which one has the greater kinetic energy: an object travelling with a velocity v or an object twice as heavy travelling with a velocity of 1/2 v?
written.finalAnswer: The object twice as heavy travelling at ½v has the greater kinetic energy; it has twice the kinetic energy of the first object.

rubric.why: The comparison must identify the object with greater kinetic energy.
rubric.how: Choose the object twice as heavy and moving at ½v.

rubric.why: Comparing the calculated energies supports the conclusion.
rubric.how: Compare ½mv² with ½(2m)(v/2)² = ½ of the first object's energy? Correct this by calculating the ratio.

modelAnswer: For the first object, Eₖ₁ = ½mv².
For the second object, Eₖ₂ = ½(2m)(½v)² = ¼mv².
Therefore, Eₖ₁ is greater; the first object has twice the kinetic energy of the second.

written.text: A car is moving along a curved road at constant speed. Does its kinetic energy change?
written.finalAnswer: No. Its kinetic energy does not change because its mass and speed remain constant.

rubric.how: State that mass and speed remain constant, so Eₖ = ½mv² stays constant.

examTips: Expect short questions asking for the definitions of energy, kinetic energy and potential energy, their SI unit, or the expressions Eₖ = ½mv² and Eₚ = mgh.
Numerical questions commonly test converting mass or velocity to SI units, substituting into an energy formula, and giving the answer with the correct unit.
For a kinetic-energy derivation, show that the work done to stop a moving body equals its kinetic energy, then reach Eₖ = ½mv².
For gravitational potential energy, show that the lifting work is wh and use w = mg to obtain Eₚ = mgh.
In comparisons, remember that kinetic energy depends on the square of speed, while gravitational potential energy depends on height.

explain.title: Energy
explain.body: Energy can be defined as the ability of a body to do work. Energy is a scalar quantity, and its SI unit is joule (J). When work is done, energy is transferred to the body on which the work is done.

explain.title: Kinetic energy
explain.body: The kinetic energy of a body is the energy that a body possesses by virtue of its motion. The work needed to stop a moving body equals its kinetic energy. For mass m and velocity v, Eₖ = ½mv².

explain.title: Potential energy
explain.body: Potential energy is defined as the energy that a body possesses by virtue of its position or deformation. A raised body has gravitational potential energy because work was done to lift it.

explain.title: Gravitational potential energy
explain.body: The work done to lift a body at constant velocity is its weight multiplied by the height: Eₚ = wh. Since w = mg, the relation becomes Eₚ = mgh.

mistakes: Using grams instead of kilograms, or km h⁻¹ instead of m s⁻¹, in an energy calculation.
Forgetting that velocity is squared in Eₖ = ½mv².
Using Eₚ = mgh but leaving out g or the height.
Writing an answer without its unit, or confusing joules (energy) with newtons (force).
Assuming that a change in direction changes kinetic energy when speed and mass stay constant.
When comparing kinetic energies, forgetting that a change in speed is squared.
